questions.q:
A designer is looking to produce a new line of environmentally-friendly washing machines.

Which of the following would be the major focus for the designer?
options: Operational capabilities
Water-saving capabilities
How much the product will cost consumers
Whether the product will appeal to the target market
questions.explanation: An environmentally-friendly product is defined by its impact on resources, so reducing water use is the major design factor here. Cost, market appeal and general operation matter to any product but are not the environmental focus driving this design.

questions.q: Why does a designer conduct market research?
options: To increase brand awareness
To increase the number of sales
To better understand their client
To identify the needs for the intended design
questions.explanation: Market research gathers information about the target market so the designer can identify the needs the design must satisfy. Brand awareness and sales are marketing outcomes, not the purpose of the research itself.

questions.q:
A design for a new shopping centre food court has been commissioned.

At what stage of the design process would the designer first create a CAD model?
options: Initial contact with clients
Brainstorming potential ideas
Presentation of ideas for feedback
Reflection of feedback and changes to design
questions.explanation: A CAD model is a developed representation used to communicate a refined idea, so it is first created when presenting ideas to the client for feedback. Initial contact and brainstorming come too early for a formal CAD model.

questions.q: Why do designers establish and review 'criteria to evaluate success' when designing?
options: To increase the number of sales of a product
To ensure environmental factors are considered
To ensure the final design meets the specified needs
To maintain product awareness for further refinement of innovative products
questions.explanation: Criteria to evaluate success are measurable benchmarks drawn from the design brief, used to check the final design meets the specified needs. The other options are narrower commercial or environmental concerns, not the overall purpose of evaluation criteria.

questions.q: In designing a suitable aid for the ageing population, a designer would first consider that the end product is
options: durable and well made.
cost effective and easy to store.
aesthetically pleasing and easy to use.
able to meet a need and be ergonomically designed.
questions.explanation: The first consideration for any aid is that it meets the identified need and is ergonomically suited to the user's physical capabilities. Durability, storage and aesthetics are secondary to function and ergonomics for an ageing user.

questions.q: Within the design process, social media can best be used as
options: a form of communication.
an innovative design practice.
a current digital design technique.
an acceptable industrial procedure.
questions.explanation: Social media is a channel for sharing ideas and gathering feedback, so within the design process it functions as a form of communication. It is not itself a design technique or a manufacturing procedure.

questions.q:
People have moved from capturing holiday memories using a digital SLR camera, which has the single function of taking photos, to a multifunctional smartphone with a camera application.

A reason for this shift to using smartphones is most likely to be the
options: convenience of capturing experiences.
obsolescence of single function cameras.
capability to capture higher quality images.
process allowing for the easy digital storage of photos.
questions.explanation: A multifunctional smartphone is always carried and ready, so the most likely reason for the shift is the convenience of capturing experiences. A dedicated SLR still generally produces higher-quality images, so quality is not the driver.

questions.q: Built-in obsolescence creates opportunities for ongoing profits for companies by
options: constantly reviewing existing product lines.
incorporating technologies into the latest products.
encouraging people to change functioning products that they own.
generating a need for individuals to keep updating existing products.
questions.explanation: Built-in obsolescence designs a limited lifespan into a product so consumers must keep updating or replacing it, generating repeat sales and ongoing profit. The key is the manufactured, ongoing need to update, which option D captures.

questions.q: Who would be the person most likely to influence the features of a new sports watch?
options: A product designer
A running enthusiast
A business entrepreneur
A biomechanical engineer
questions.explanation: Features should reflect the needs of the end user, so a running enthusiast — the active user of the sports watch — is most likely to influence which features it has. The designer and engineer realise the product, but the user's needs drive the features.

questions.q: Why do information and communication technology (ICT) companies take risks with their products by supplying their software at discounted prices or free of charge to students?
options: To test the software product prior to its release to industry
To establish product familiarity in order to capture future market share
To stop illegal software piracy by students copying and sharing computer programs
To obtain personal data when the product is downloaded, and selling it to cover costs
questions.explanation: Giving software to students builds early familiarity and brand loyalty so they keep using it as paying professionals, capturing future market share. This is a long-term marketing strategy rather than testing, anti-piracy or data harvesting.

questions.q:
Question 11 (a)

Identify TWO different methods of evaluation.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies TWO different methods of evaluation

questions.modelAnswer: Two methods of evaluation are making a model (or prototype) to test the design, and surveying a niche or target market to gather user feedback.

questions.q:
Question 11 (b)

Describe how evaluation can aid the design of a product.

criteria.descriptor: Provides characteristics and features of how evaluation aids the design of a product
Sketches in general terms how evaluation aids the design of a product

questions.modelAnswer: Evaluation allows designers to test ideas before they go into full production. For example, developing a prototype lets the designer check whether the design actually works, which then provides the opportunity to make further modifications and refine the product.

questions.q:
Question 12 (4 marks)

Discuss the influence that technology can have on the design process.

criteria.descriptor: Provides points for and/or against the influence that technology can have on the design process
Describes the influence that technology can have on the design process
Outlines an influence of technology on the design process

questions.modelAnswer: Technology such as CAD/CAM can improve the designer's process. Where designers once relied on paper-based drawings, they can now 3D print a model of the object: moving from a 2D to a 3D representation shows the depth of detail and helps consumers make informed decisions about the final design. However, this technology can also bring additional costs in resources and staff training, which may negatively impact the design process.

questions.q:
Question 13 (6 marks)

Explain how changing social trends influence design practices.

criteria.descriptor: Makes evident the influences of changing social trends on design practices
Shows some relationship between changing social trends and design practices
Describes how changing social trends influence design practices
Sketches in general terms how changing social trends influence design practices

questions.modelAnswer: Changing social trends influence design practice through the uptake of the latest technology. As emerging technologies become commonplace, designers adapt their practice to make their workflow easier. For example, as the NBN trend accelerated, designers could download, work online and send much larger files from home rather than relying on a dedicated server at the workplace. Incorporating this communication trend into daily practice freed up the designer's time and removed the constraint of needing a dedicated workplace.

questions.q:
Question 14 (15 marks)

Analyse factors that could determine the success or failure of an innovative design.

Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; communicate ideas and information using relevant examples; and present a logical and cohesive response.

criteria.descriptor: Shows a comprehensive understanding of factors that help determine the success or failure of an innovative design; draws out and relates implications of those factors; provides a logical and cohesive response supported by relevant examples
Explains how factors help determine the success or failure of an innovative design; communicates using relevant examples; provides a mostly logical and cohesive response
Describes factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design; provides a mostly organised response, supported by relevant example(s)
Outlines factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design; provides example(s)
Demonstrates some understanding of factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design

questions.modelAnswer: Several factors determine whether an innovative design succeeds or fails. Successes can be driven by timing (releasing a product aligned to a seasonal change so it matches perceived consumer needs), social factors (the rising demand for meal-kit food products reflecting society's desire for convenience), and political support (government STEM-education initiatives that drive innovation). Failures can stem from available technologies (an innovation needing newer supporting technology to work, such as moving from wired headphones to Bluetooth), cultural factors (designing without considering consumers' cultural needs, e.g. supplying high technology to communities that lack electrical power), and marketing strategies (over-promising operational qualities, as with vehicle safety features recalled after causing injury). Function and aesthetics are also decisive: an electric car's batteries must meet drivers' range needs to be judged successful, while the latest phones must both look good and display information attractively (e.g. wrap-around screens) or consumers will turn to competitors. A strong response analyses how these interacting factors combine to determine the success or failure of the innovation.
